config.title: Build sandboxed code runner safe eval strategy

intro.title: Build sandboxed code runner safe eval strategy
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a safe, sandboxed code runner that can execute user-provided JavaScript without risking your main application. You'll learn how to use the Function constructor to create isolated execution contexts, which helps prevent access to global variables and dangerous APIs. The core programming concept involves creating a controlled environment (a sandbox) to run untrusted code securely. You'll work with JavaScript's built-in Function constructor and learn strategies to limit its capabilities for safety. By the end, you'll have a basic but functional safe eval strategy that can run code snippets securely.
intro.usecase: This sandboxed code runner pattern is essential for any application that allows users to execute custom code safely. You'll see it in online code playgrounds like CodePen or JSFiddle, where users can write and test JavaScript without compromising the hosting platform. It's also critical in educational platforms like freeCodeCamp or Codecademy, where learners submit code exercises that need isolated evaluation. Additionally, dashboard builders and CMS systems use this approach to safely execute custom widget logic or user-defined formulas without risking the main application's security.

objectives: Construct a sandboxed environment using iframe isolation techniques
Implement a secure message-passing interface between parent window and sandbox
Configure a restricted eval function that prevents access to global objects
Apply input sanitization to filter potentially dangerous code patterns
Initialize a code execution controller with timeout and error boundaries
Integrate a result validation layer to verify output safety
Manipulate the execution context to limit available APIs and methods

steps.title: Import required modules
steps.instruction: Import the 'vm' module from Node.js to create isolated JavaScript environments.
steps.hint: Use the CommonJS require syntax to import the built-in 'vm' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a built-in Node.js module
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The vm module is imported and ready to use for sandboxed code execution.
successCriteria: The vm module is imported using require('vm').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing the 'vm' module specifically. Check the syntax for importing built-in Node.js modules.
steps.feedbackWrong: The vm module isn't imported correctly. Remember to use require('vm') to import this built-in Node.js module for sandboxed execution.

steps.title: Create main function structure
steps.instruction: Create a function called 'safeEval' that accepts a code string as its parameter. The function body can be empty for now.
steps.hint: Define a function with the name 'safeEval' that takes one parameter (e.g., 'code' or 'codeString').

successCriteria: The safeEval function exists and accepts a code string parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a function named 'safeEval' that takes one parameter (like 'code').
steps.feedbackWrong: The safeEval function isn't properly defined. Create a function with that exact name that accepts a code string parameter.

steps.title: Initialize sandbox context
steps.instruction: Inside your safeEval function, create a new sandbox context using vm.createContext() with an empty object and assign it to a variable named sandboxContext.
steps.hint: Use vm.createContext({}) to create an isolated execution environment with no initial global properties.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an isolated context for safe execution
const sandboxContext = vm.createContext({});
steps.expectedOutcome: The safeEval function will have a sandboxContext variable initialized with an empty VM context.
successCriteria: A sandboxContext variable is created inside safeEval using vm.createContext({}).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using vm.createContext() with an empty object {} inside your safeEval function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sandbox context wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use vm.createContext({}) inside your safeEval function.

steps.title: Define execution timeout
steps.instruction: Inside the safeEval function, define a timeout constant set to 5000 milliseconds.
steps.hint: Add a variable declaration like `const timeout = 5000;` inside the function body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The safeEval function will have a timeout constant defined to limit execution time.
successCriteria: The safeEval function contains a constant named 'timeout' with value 5000.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a constant named 'timeout' with value 5000 inside the safeEval function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timeout constant isn't defined correctly. Add `const timeout = 5000;` inside the safeEval function.

steps.title: Create safe execution wrapper
steps.instruction: Inside the safeEval function, create a try-catch block to wrap the code execution logic you'll add later.
steps.hint: Add try { } catch (error) { } inside your function body. You can leave the try block empty for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: The safeEval function now has a try-catch structure ready to handle execution errors.
successCriteria: The safeEval function contains a try-catch block structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added both the try and catch blocks inside the safeEval function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The try-catch block is missing. Remember to add try { } catch (error) { } inside your safeEval function.

steps.title: Execute code in sandbox
steps.instruction: Inside the safeEval function's try block, use vm.runInContext() to execute the code string within the sandbox context and store the result in a variable.
steps.hint: Call vm.runInContext(code, sandbox) where 'code' is the user-provided code string and 'sandbox' is the isolated context you created earlier.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: executing code in an isolated context
const result = vm.runInContext(userCode, isolatedContext);
steps.expectedOutcome: The user's code will be executed within the isolated sandbox environment using vm.runInContext().
successCriteria: vm.runInContext() is called inside the try block with the code string and sandbox context as arguments, and the result is stored in a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling vm.runInContext() with both the code string and sandbox context as arguments inside the try block.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code execution step is missing. You need to use vm.runInContext() to run the user code in the sandbox context.

steps.title: Handle execution results
steps.instruction: Inside the safeEval function, after the try-catch block, return the result from the sandbox execution. If there is no result, return null.
steps.hint: You can return the value captured from the vm.runInContext call. If an error occurred, the catch block should handle it, but you still need to return something from the function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The safeEval function should return the evaluated result of the code or null if execution failed.
successCriteria: The safeEval function returns the result from the sandbox execution or null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to return the result from the sandbox execution. If there's no result, return null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The safeEval function should return the result from the sandbox execution or null. Check your return statement.

steps.title: Implement error handling
steps.instruction: Inside the catch block, return an error object with the error message property.
steps.hint: In the catch block, you can return an object like { error: error.message }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The catch block now returns an error object containing the error message.
successCriteria: The catch block returns an object with an error property containing the error message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your catch block returns an object with an error property containing the error message.

steps.title: Add input validation
steps.instruction: At the beginning of your safeEval function, add validation to check if the 'code' parameter is a non-empty string. If it's not, return an error object immediately.
steps.hint: Use an if statement to check if code is falsy or not a string. Return an object with an error property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The safeEval function will now validate its input before attempting execution, preventing errors from malformed or missing code.
successCriteria: The function includes validation that checks if 'code' is a non-empty string and returns an error object when validation fails.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some validation, but make sure to check both that code exists AND is a string type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The validation is missing or incomplete. Add an if statement at the function start to validate the 'code' parameter.

steps.title: Test the safeEval function
steps.instruction: Call the safeEval function with a simple JavaScript expression like '2 + 2' and log the result to the console.
steps.hint: Add a console.log statement at the end of your code that calls safeEval with a string argument containing valid JavaScript.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console should display the result of evaluating the JavaScript expression you passed to safeEval.
successCriteria: safeEval is called with a valid JavaScript expression string and the result is logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
